column2: From Mexico, Olson lets his favorite students, including the painter Fielding Dawson, know that he wants to come back; the students take up a collection to pay for his trip. Student collection Consequences: The return of Olson, the college's future leader

To celebrate Olson's return, Shahn (glyph paintings), the dancer Katherine Litz (an interpretation of the poem in movement), and Lou Harrison (a score for prepared piano) create a performance around a poem by Olson lashing out at the materialist basis of American life. Score: someone presses hard against all the low strings with a piece of heavy wood about 2 x 2 inches, set on edge at a “nodal angle” Consequences: An ideal celebration of Olson's vision
Photograph by Jonathan Williams showing Olson at the college in 1951 writing The Maximus Poems; Olson, the last rector and the guiding influence of the 1950s. Photograph by Jonathan Williams

Olson, in town with Alvin Lipsey, the young nephew of the college's Black cook, comes upon a local auction. The boy exclaims: “It's like a race”. Olson, struck by the echo of slave auctions, writes a short, supposedly spontaneous poem dedicated to “Alvin and the Shahns” and gives it to Ben Shahn, there for the summer. The child's exclamation; dedication “Alvin and the Shahns” Consequences: Sets off the exchange of glyphs

Shahn answers Olson's poem with A Glyph for Charles, painted in a palimpsest style without erasures. Lou Harrison (Cage's associate, hired in his absence) composes The Glyph for prepared piano, 2 bells, claves, tuning fork, and perhaps a gong, offered to Katherine Litz, who choreographs a dance to the score with an enlarged version of Shahn's painting as the main set. Instrumentation: “prepared piano, 2 bells, claves, pitch fork, & perhaps, gong”; each contribution produced separately but quickly Consequences: A model of spontaneous interdisciplinary collaboration

After two years of Turner, two other Alfred graduates, Karnes and her husband Weinrib, take over; they have few serious students, among them M.C. Richards. Karnes's work is judged too functional by some; Weinrib is more experimental, building from slabs of clay.

In a famous lecture, de Kooning voices his weariness with all the orthodoxies of modern art and declares “I do not need a movement”, an echo of the unease some Black Mountain students felt toward the research Albers promoted.

A play for two actors (the dancer: Apollonius; the voice: Tyana, or the place), illustrated with a map by Stan VanDerBeek (“map of moves”), printed and bound at the college in the summer of 1951, in original two-color boards. 8vo, two-color boards, VanDerBeek map
Her first poem-images date from 1951, made while she was waiting for the birth of her son Christopher.

After Christopher's birth, Weil briefly comes back to join Rauschenberg at Black Mountain; Motherwell and Shahn are teaching there that summer. She takes part in campus life without being a student, with a marriage coming apart and a colicky baby; she produces almost nothing. Consequences: End of Weil's direct tie to the college

After the last devastating faculty quarrel, around 1951, Bill Levi leaves for Washington University, taking their young daughter Estelle; perhaps the lowest point for M.C., which no one talks about, no doubt to her relief. Washington University Consequences: A very difficult situation for M.C.

One afternoon, she confesses to being jealous that Dawson has not yet read Moby Dick and can read it for the first time; an admission of honesty whose worth, for him, equals that of the book. An office looking out on the lake Consequences: Dawson discovers what she meant: a first experience without equal after Don Quixote

In the early 1950s, a Container Corporation of America advertisement shows a brilliant watercolor by Philip Guston that astonishes them: proof that creative art could make its way into the world of advertising, a hope soon belied. Consequences: A clear-eyed illusion: their art had an effect, but always within the system

The two young artists, watched by Motherwell, who had come to teach that summer, threw handfuls of pebbles at a large canvas mostly covered with tar; Motherwell, between them, gestured for more, again and again, and they kept throwing. A large canvas mostly covered with tar; handfuls of pebbles; gravel patio
When the model did not show up, Bob and Cy got up from their drawing boards, walked to the front of the class, and began to undress.

Dawson discovers Melville's The Confidence-Man in 1951, finds it dry, then loves it; through the winter days and nights, on his mattress in his study, he rereads it endlessly; chapter 33 (p. 215, Grove Press edition) shows him what he wanted: fiction must present another world to which one nonetheless feels the tie. Chapter 33, page 215, Grove Press paperback edition. Consequences: The book becomes a major influence on Dawson.

For his fortieth birthday, Goodman writes an essay judging his literary career a failure: no audience won over; it is time to do something else. Consequences: He begins seeing patients as a Gestalt therapist

Goodman, who helped Fritz and Lore Perls theorize Gestalt therapy (a blend of psychoanalysis and existentialism), takes on patients. Sessions at one or two dollars; $1,000 earned that year, on top of his wife's secretarial salary; decent poverty still possible in New York in 1951

Goodman doubts his strength and enters a decade he calls “a useless time”; he challenges himself to find an ounce more strength and finishes the fourth volume of The Empire City with no hope of finding a publisher. Personal challenge: an ounce more strength; manuscript finished with no publisher in sight Consequences: Completion of The Empire City
On the occasion of his second exhibition, he says he did not feel ready for exhibitions, is not particularly happy with this one, and still works out of doubt.
In the summer of 1951, M.C. Richards and the choreographer Katherine Litz revive the circus-style, in-the-round events inherited from the Jennerjahns.

A turning-point score: in composing, Cage asks questions about the features of the score, then tosses coins or draws the traditional yarrow stalks to build the hexagrams required by the I Ching; the “answers” determine the duration, tempo, and other dynamics of the composition. He uses only the randomizing structure, not the divinatory aspect. Coins, yarrow stalks, hexagrams of the I Ching (Book of Changes) Consequences: A turning point in Cage's compositional method, later applied to Theater Piece No. 1

Cage expects total silence but hears two sounds, one high and one low; the engineer explains that the high one is his nervous system and the low one his blood circulating. A soundproof anechoic chamber Consequences: Cage locates there the possibility of composing 4'33"
David Tudor comes to Black Mountain for the first time in 1951 as piano accompanist to the dancer Katherine Litz; he is also there in the summer of 1952.
Fuller coins the phrase “Spaceship Earth” in 1951; it will later appear on the cover of Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth (1963)

In the fall, Excavation receives the Logan purchase prize at the Art Institute of Chicago's annual exhibition. Purchase prize from the Frank G. Logan Prize Fund Consequences: A little money and visibility for the group

More than a quarter century after arriving at the Bauhaus (thus around 1951, about twenty-six years after 1922-1923), Anni writes the account of her arrival and of Gropius's welcoming speech to the new students. She recalls the vestal white garments, the shabby baggy dresses and suits, a homemade touch; Gropius's speech lasted an hour; she compares it with Gropius's opening address at Harvard the year before, reported by young friends

Revering Gorky, Elaine writes a superb analysis of his work and life; few critics at the time had probed so penetratingly the meaning of his painting and the dark, obscure sides of his life. In her notes she writes, among other things, that Gorky, unlike Mondrian, loved the history of painting, saw Walt Disney, the coldness of lavender neon, the garish tones of Technicolor, traffic lights, neon signs; he could “see plants grow.” Notes for the article preserved; sentence: “he could see plants grow”. Consequences: According to Elaine, Harold Rosenberg will draw from it the idea of the artist using his own life, a year before his article on the Action Painters.

One spring evening, the author passes a young woman in black, a black lace shawl over red-gold hair, huge eyes, luminous white skin, bright red lips, walking fast without seeing her, swept along toward what was probably a party. Black outfit, black lace shawl, red-gold hair, red lips Consequences: The friend with her identifies her: “That must be Elaine de Kooning”
Newly arrived in New York, Elise Asher is overwhelmed by the two women, so learned, so strong, so absolutely sure of themselves, so central; she cannot say a word in front of them.
The Whitney gives Gorky a retrospective covering two decades of his work. Consequences: Despite Greenberg's glowing article in The Nation, Gorky remains little accepted by the general public.

A fifty-six-year-old painter, largely self-taught, of graceful still lifes and serene classical figures; a former commercial artist (theater signs from the age of fourteen, in the days of Mae Murray), a military newspaper illustrator during World War I, a poster artist for Warner Brothers. A six-story whale for Moby Dick repainted as a zeppelin the following week; his first patron, Jules Mastbaum, founder of the Rodin Museum in Philadelphia, paid for his first trip to Paris

Davis writes that he divides all art, past and present, into two major categories: objective (absolute art, which sees the percept of the real world as an immediate event) and subjective (illustration through symbols and emotional detours). Davis's formula for subjective art: “the character of a Universal Bellyache” and “a Perverse Passion for the Detour”.
Ten years after the purchase, Graham offers the painting to Bill for five hundred dollars; Bill buys it back. $500, against $50 in 1940

A quarrel at the retrospective leads Elaine to recommend Porter to Thomas Hess for ARTnews; Porter writes to a friend that she spoke to him about the quality of his writing and he about its mediocrity; he gets the critic's post Elaine had held. Consequences: Porter takes over Elaine's critic slot when she moves on to feature articles

Before Williams drives off to Asheville, Harrison asks for his bottle of Rock and Rye; Williams obliges, amazed that anyone could like this syrupy liqueur. Words: Harrison asks for a bottle of Rock and Rye; Williams comments on the drink's repulsive sweetness. Atmosphere: Summer friendship, a Sunday drive, a comedy of taste Stakes: A small ritual of friendship that fixes a character

When an intense self-revelation satisfies him, Olson slowly rises from his chair, towers over the author, shouts his enthusiasm, and fixes the newly chosen one with fierce affection. Victor, author of the line “I finger my innards for the truth”, becomes the hero of the workshop for the week, until the next raw metaphor. Words: “Si, Victor, si! You have it, Victor!” Atmosphere: adoration, competition for the master's ear Stakes: The making of disciples; an economy of favor

After reading Gray's stories (the persona of a middle-aged alcoholic actor seeking salvation in a Bowery church), Olson thunders: pure shit; she is forbidden to write anything but a journal, at least an hour a day, for a year, and is to come back the following summer. He nonetheless spares these dreadful texts any public humiliation. Words: “Girl, this is pure shit! You're going to do nothing but keep a journal for a year, an hour a day minimum...” Atmosphere: the mentor's salutary violence Stakes: The birth of a woman writer through the destruction of her models

Olson, in a serape over his bare chest, sits down next to Cage in a black suit and tie; a laconic conversation, punctuated by the Zen laugh of Cage as he ponders his next Happening Atmosphere: a striking contrast of dress; cultivated terseness Stakes: an emblematic image of the college: two aesthetics side by side

Unloading an old Ford; Rauschenberg notices a bundle of small canvases covered with zinc white; he holds one at arm's length and exclaims enthusiastically that it is really an interesting painting; the original shapes show through the white Words: “What's this! … This is really an interesting painting.” Atmosphere: The painter's immediate enthusiasm, the bewilderment of the newcomer, who saw in them only material to recycle Stakes: The accident of covering over becomes art: an opening lesson for the newcomer

Sitting on the steps, Twombly helps Rauschenberg brush white paint over a series of stretched canvases Atmosphere: Calm work outdoors, a few days after the witness's arrival Stakes: The birth of the future White Paintings before the eyes of a witness who does not yet know it

The evening class runs from 7 p.m. to 11 p.m.; everyone stops at Ma Peak's tavern to load up on beer; back at the college for a session that lasts all night and the following day; then back to Peak's the second night Atmosphere: exuberance, beer, inexhaustible talk Stakes: Olson's teaching as a collective fever

Wes reads the whole adaptation aloud, “gamely”; he and Duck exchange looks of compassionate tolerance before a transcription with no dramaturgy Atmosphere: A sparse room around the big table; a lesson received gently Stakes: An apprentice writer's failure, before Olson's teaching

Pollock gets drunk, shouts, comes close to violence; Lee reasons with him like a child in a tantrum until he sinks into a stupor; then she shows Hartigan the work and sells her husband as a genius; Pollock, loosened by drink, declares there are only two guys in town, Pollock and de Kooning, and sends Hartigan to see the Egan show. Words: Pollock: “There are only two guys in town… Pollock and de Kooning”; “Tell him I sent you.” Atmosphere: Smoldering violence, then motherly calming; the young painter's admiration. Stakes: The passing of the torch and the seed of the rivalry.

Hartigan knocks at the door; Bill sticks his head out the window (“Who's dat?” “Come on up, den”); they look at the canvases, and Bill speaks well of Jackson; Elaine bursts in, flirts with Bill, asks him for money for a coat; he objects that he already gave her some, and she has spent it all; Hartigan leaves without knowing how the crisis is resolved. Words: Bill: “Yah, Jackson is something”; an exchange about the money for the coat. Atmosphere: Charming, close, suddenly domestic and awkward. Stakes: A portrait of the de Kooning couple and of Elaine's place.

The child, having learned the word doggie and been rewarded for it, applies it to every four-legged animal; to point out a horse to his mother he cries that he sees a big doggie; she corrects him and shows him the distinguishing features; little by little he acquires a precise vocabulary for everything that strikes his exteroceptors and his tutor's at the same time. Words: The child calls the horse a big doggie, and his mother answers that it is a horse. Stakes: How the precision of public language is born, and why private language cannot be born that way.

Walking with his mother on a scorching sidewalk, the child says he prefers the shadows, in a metaphor that convention has not yet emasculated. Words: “I like the shadows better. The sun makes a noise in my stomach.” Atmosphere: Crushing heat, shade sought out, a child's voice free of cliché. Stakes: A child's perception before conventional language.

Electrodes taped to the forehead track the potentials of the frontal muscle; the tonus drops, proprioception falls below the critical threshold, sleep comes; the relay trips, the buzzer sounds, the man starts and wakes up: he has woken himself by falling asleep. Stakes: External control of the body up to the threshold of sleep.

A first attempt (~15 minutes) broken off by growing impatience; the word “now” gives a feeling of immediacy, accompanied by fear (deep breathing, tightness in the chest); he suddenly sees objects he had only glanced at, feels an urge to tidy up, the objects stand around him with no continuity with him; second attempt: the same fear, a tendency to label the objects with adjectives instead of experiencing the act of observing; third attempt, in the subway: less fear because of the other people, vision multiplied a hundredfold, keen pleasure, then an amusing game, but costly in energy. Words: A report written by the student, quoted at length by the authors Atmosphere: The isolation of the room, objects seen as if for the first time; a subway crowd that soothes and stimulates Stakes: The fear of being truly alive and present

One gives up one's usual reading; one looks around and says to oneself: the train is swaying, people are heading for the exit, that man is looking at me, I am worried about the impression I make. Words: “At this moment I am riding in the subway. Now the train is swaying…” Atmosphere: The lulling rhythm of the car, an anonymous crowd Stakes: Keeping in touch with the here and now

After the reversal exercise, a student writes that after years of shapeless opinions in which he felt like a lost soul, he has at last forged opinions through experience and would rather be rigid than an amoeba; the precision of a decision counts for more than a state of chronic analysis; one cannot depart too publicly from the consensus without ending up committed to a state hospital. Words: He concludes that there is a limit to the odd behavior one can allow oneself before ending up committed. Atmosphere: Defensive, ironic; the fear of the asylum shows through. Stakes: The resistance to the exercise reveals precisely the inner conflict the exercise was looking for.

Reversing letters (“p” into “q”) disturbs this student as much as seeing someone open a can or a pack of cigarettes upside down; he cannot fall asleep if a drawer is open or the closet door not shut. Words: Things must be exactly as they ought to be, that is, the right way. Atmosphere: Obsessive unease, a need for order. Stakes: The exercise touches the neurotic knot of order.

Trying to imagine words turned around, the student grows nervous: her heart races, her eyes water; she then tries writing the letters backward, but her eyes burn so much that she can no longer look. Words: She protests that it is crazy and asks what the authors are doing to them with these experiments. Atmosphere: Real physiological anxiety: racing heart, tears. Stakes: The harmless visual exercise sets off a bodily panic reaction, proof that the resistance is there.

His fiancée is coming back from Europe after nearly nine months; they are going to be married and he can hardly sit still. Asked to imagine opposite wishes, he writes that he does not want her back, does not love her, would rather chase other girls for a few more years, and recognizes some truth in this last point. He then gets angry at the authors and attacks their algebraic account of zero, then, his aggression having been expressed directly, concedes that his objections were perhaps very personal. Words: He objects that the truth of a situation is spread over the whole continuum; one side is not all positive or all negative. Atmosphere: Official euphoria, then disappointment, aggressiveness, and finally calm. Stakes: The exercise brings out a refused truth; anger at the experimenter is the logical sequel to the insight.

He is eagerly awaiting the child he and his wife have planned; invited to imagine being unable to bear the prospect, he lists, with an ease that surprises him, loss of freedom, getting up in the middle of the night, medical expenses, and other drawbacks. Words: He concludes that there are no credits without debits. Atmosphere: Clear-eyed eagerness, surprise at himself. Stakes: Anticipating the debits of an awaited happiness.

A student reverses situations in which she had gotten angry at people. Words: Some of them made her laugh out loud; there was relief, as if she were done with them. Atmosphere: Release, laughter, discharge. Stakes: Reversal as the completion of a blocked emotion.

They take turns suggesting situations to reverse and all goes well, until the mother proposes reversing the mother-daughter relationship; the student's imagination dries up completely Words: the mother suggests the mother-daughter reversal; the student: “my imagination dried up completely” Atmosphere: a shared game, then a sudden break Stakes: showing the border where imagination touches the family taboo

She imagines being a waitress seated at a table while a customer serves her; though she knows it is unreal, she feels the muscles of her legs tense to inhibit the urge to get up and set the situation right Words: her account of the muscular tension in her legs Atmosphere: a body reacting to fiction Stakes: imagination vivid enough to trigger motor behavior

While waiting for someone or for a bus, let figures and grounds be freely seen and heard, then, without forcing, let oneself be flooded by the feeling of the meaningless chaos of the surroundings, and note the resistances Words: “I am now impatient” Atmosphere: the rising anxiety of waiting, surroundings coming apart Stakes: converting sterile impatience into creative pre-engagement in the actual situation

Unable to put into words her emotions and tastes before inert objects, she begins attributing emotions to them at random; these gradually become real, to the point that she almost forgets their arbitrary character. Words: “It sort of scared me to see how easily I could fool myself”. Atmosphere: Initial doubt before neutral objects; then a clear-eyed unease. Stakes: The fragile border between feigned and real emotion.

The student does the emotional differentiation exercise in a crowded subway and discovers considerable aggressiveness toward the other passengers; instead of being ashamed of it, he enjoys it and wants to tell them what he thinks of them; later, in a less irritating setting, he goes over the scene again and then experiences the blocks (shame, a wish to water it down) that were expected but absent at the time. Words: He admits that he rather enjoyed this aggressiveness. Atmosphere: Crowding, irritation, then a cooler look back. Stakes: True emotion surfaces when it can; shame comes afterward.

Sitting near his father-in-law, with whom he has always been on excellent terms, the man puts into words that he loves him and feels a vague anxiety rising, a sense that he hates something in that face; he breaks off the experiment, then understands that it is a fear reaction, fed by his wife's and sister-in-law's stories of their father's harshness in their childhood, a fear with nothing concrete behind it. Words: The anxiety put into words: he hates something in that face. Atmosphere: Surface affection, underground unease. Stakes: Emotion inherited by hearsay against the actual relationship.

Her husband demands that she listen when he develops a theory, even when the children are up to something potentially serious; torn between the pride of answering intelligently and protecting the children, she feels anger and frustration, then the conflict becomes intolerable and is resolved by turning all her attention to the children. Words: The “chaos of divided attention”. Atmosphere: Domestic tension, being pulled both ways. Stakes: The impossible choice between the theorizing husband and the children in danger.

Always a little contemptuous of his friend's pride of ownership (a Cadillac owned and cherished for more than a year, in which he has often ridden), the man focuses his attention on the car and for the first time really notices its beautiful lines, curves, and functional capacities; he draws an unexpected aesthetic emotion from it, and his pleasure is outdone by his friend's when he sincerely and spontaneously compliments the beauty of the car. Words: “A small incident, perhaps”, but a sign of the new areas of experience that true awareness opens up. Atmosphere: Initial contempt melting into admiration; shared pleasure. Stakes: Giving in to an admiration one had refused on principle.

Lying on a couch, the subject states each awareness: he is lying down, he wants to do the experiment, he hesitates over where to begin, the radio is playing in the next room (it reminds him of the program he wanted to hear), he catches himself, feels lost, remembers the advice to stay on the surface, feels his crossed legs, a pain in his back, the urge to change position, then changes position Words: “Now I am aware that I am lying on the couch… the radio is playing in the next room.” Atmosphere: Fluid inwardness, interruptions, self-correction Stakes: Showing the method in action, with its misfires

Sitting in a train, a subject explores his internal sensations, reaches the region of the rectum, and finds its muscles clenched as tight as they can be, with no urge to move his bowels, as if he were holding his breath with his lower colon; he also finds a band of tension at the level of the navel; since then he checks this tension automatically when walking, standing, or lying down, and always finds it, wondering whether his concentration is not creating it Words: The subject finds this tension silly and wonders how he can know that it is not his concentration that calls it up Atmosphere: Intimate astonishment, embarrassed curiosity Stakes: The body reveals what the will did not know

During the experiment, a man suddenly finds he has no use for his arms: he crosses them awkwardly over his chest, puts them in his pockets, feels ill at ease, squirms, feels confused, gets up almost at once, and walks around; his wife calls him to dinner and he is glad to give up the experiment Atmosphere: Growing embarrassment, a relieved escape Stakes: Resistance disguised as restlessness; domestic life as a way out

After three weeks without results, a subject suddenly becomes aware of his muscular tensions and feels like “a mass of knotted muscle”: the small of his back, the back of his neck, the tops of his legs; his mind fixes on a small irritation until it blots out the rest of the body; he concludes that resistances and tensions are one and the same thing, and understands his tension verbally without being able to release it Words: “I was a mass of knotted muscle” Atmosphere: Dread and fascination Stakes: The threshold at which the body reveals itself as foreign

During the body-awareness experiment, he does not know what to do with his arms, crosses them over his chest, puts them in his pockets, squirms, feels confused, gets up, walks around the room; his wife calls him to dinner and he is relieved to give up. Words: “I am glad to leave the experiment”. Atmosphere: Domestic unease, feverish restlessness, the relief of escape. Stakes: The body reveals a desire that consciousness refuses to see.

During the exercise, his thoughts stop, he clenches his fists, his chest swells as if to shout something he cannot identify; a month later, he delivers an effective dressing-down to his fiancée's overly meddlesome parents. Atmosphere: Mute tension, then delayed release. Stakes: The blocked emotion finds its real addressee in life.

Rereading his notes before typing them, the subject feels his neck stiff, his lower lip tight, and his breathing heavy, the pattern of holding back resentment; at the very moment he breaks into a broad smile, he realizes that he felt exploited and martyred at having to do these experiments, and that his anger at the experimenter had finally arrived. Words: “The resentment toward you had finally arrived!” Atmosphere: A discovery both comic and liberating; since then the exercise leaves him refreshed and collected. Stakes: The transfer of anger onto the experimenter is finally admitted.

During the experiment on habits, a man notes that he can innovate in his behavior only at the price of feeling very unlucky; he hides his superstition and discovers that he resents anyone who makes him take a different path. Words: He admits that in following the other person's path he feels miserable and furious with himself, and only now realizes that he resents the other person and feels that person owes him a great deal. Atmosphere: The tone of an astonished confession, of discovery in the heat of the moment. Stakes: The moment one sees one's own secret mechanism for the first time.

A man watches his wife iron one of his shirts with a care he does not have; his own system favors speed, and he gets irritated as if he were pushing the iron faster himself. Words: He says he felt tense pushing the iron, annoyed by her slowness. Atmosphere: Domestic, microscopic, revealing. Stakes: The confluence between two ways of doing things, even in a tiny gesture.

A subject feels compelled to close the doors others leave open; if he tries to ignore an open door, he sits in anxiety until it is closed. Words: He says that getting up to close the door is less uncomfortable than waiting for someone else to do it. Atmosphere: Smoldering tension, physical discomfort. Stakes: The compulsion that governs the most ordinary gestures.

A man describes a whole life reduced to systems of habits (combing his hair before shaving so that the moisture does not run onto the talc) to save time for the serious business of thinking; he has eliminated certain rituals, but changing even an efficient habit makes him anxious, and he cannot help coaching anyone who goes about things differently. Words: He jokes that his superego nags his ego until “we” do something. Atmosphere: Clear-eyed irony about himself. Stakes: The intellectual who systematizes his life and monitors other people's.

An isolated student, unable to make contact with his dormitory mates, hears from his room the others being called outside by their friends; one night he is found under his own window, calling his own name over and over Words: He calls himself the way one calls someone outside Atmosphere: Night, pathetic loneliness tinged with absurdity Stakes: A perfect image of retroflection: giving oneself what one wanted to receive from others

At the moment the patient should voice a reproach, he feels the attack rising, does not dare, turns it against himself, feels hurt, and bursts into tears, sometimes several times in a session. Words: The tears seem to say: see how harmless and mistreated I am. Atmosphere: The damp heat of repeated outbursts, chronic resentment. Stakes: Aggression cannot be reorganized outward as long as the circuit stays looped back on the self.

Typing her report, she feels a nervous irritation that starts in her legs and spreads through her whole body; she scratches, pounds the keys, her left arm stiffens to the bone; a letter from her parents tightens her throat; she admits she cries easily at a movie but never in her personal relationships; the aggressiveness returns, the pain in her left arm returns Words: She reflects that one plays many roles in a life and wonders which is the real one that represents the self; she refuses to allow herself the luxury of crying Atmosphere: A pounded typewriter, a body tearing itself apart, held-back anger and tears Stakes: An unresolved conflict with parents who do not accept her way of life; guilt over a refused return home

Lying down, he makes contact with his body, breathes deeply, feels the excitement rise and ebb; he holds back his breathing, so he pants deliberately: the excitement runs through him in bolts of electricity, his body twists in every direction, burning, sweating, in tears, crying “Ohh...” for several minutes; afterward he looks at his hands to see whether they are scorched; shivers for half an hour, a feeling of strength Words: He looked at his hands to see whether they were burned and would not have been surprised to find they were. Atmosphere: The heat of fire, hands and feet ablaze, sobs and groans Stakes: The promise and the fear of what these experiments release; the honeymoon phase may not last

Weariness with the overrated pseudo-crime: he declares that none of his impulses trouble him, that he does not fear his wish to kill, that he shouts loudly but spares the neighbors, then accuses himself: he is no doubt a psychopathic personality; he has stolen cars, taken drugs, lived with women; and he dares them to prove it. Words: He claims to be ashamed of nothing, absolutely nothing, about himself. Atmosphere: Provocation, mocking defiance Stakes: Resistance under cover of total transparency

Alone at home for once, he pushes the table aside, lies down first fully dressed (embarrassed), then undresses completely on a blanket; his rapid breathing calms; an erection he involuntarily tries to curb, and at once a backache; he begins to put two and two together; comparing his two sides: right shoulder raised, weight on the left shoulder and buttock; an irresistible urge to stretch, then a wrestler's bridge on his feet and the back of his neck; on coming back down to the floor, a strange relief, the small of his back closer to the floor Words: this pain “is an old acquaintance”; overall sense: he no longer feels so confused Atmosphere: excitement, intimacy, discovery Stakes: the body reveals the link between sexual defense and chronic pain

Lying down, she becomes aware of her shame about her genitals and of a strong urge to cover them with her hand; a memory of her mother: “nice girls never expose themselves”; an upbringing weighing on moral virtue, warnings, and sermons; she concludes that there is a great deal of “unfinished business,” but a good start Words: the mother: “nice girls never expose themselves” Atmosphere: shame, dawning lucidity Stakes: the conflict between natural desire and prohibitions implanted in childhood

His father rebukes him sharply when he knows he is in the right; jaw and throat knotted, a cry held back; he feels he must not hurt his father, and that is precisely what he does by grumbling afterward; resolution: next time, speak his mind Words: the father demands to know what is eating him; the son cannot let any of it out Atmosphere: contained tension Stakes: moving from wounding silence to direct speech

Tension in the diaphragm, a subtle urge to vomit, convulsive hiccups; his hands clench almost spontaneously, his head shakes no, and the word bursts out loud and charged with emotion; he goes as far as strangling the pillow and sees intimate visual images he refuses to describe; the tensions in the diaphragm do not return Words: “no” said aloud, “quite loudly and with much emotion” Atmosphere: cathartic discharge Stakes: the body succeeds where speech did not dare

During a muscle-tension experiment, a pain in his arm spreads through his whole body; the man trembles with fear, wants to reach out his arms toward someone (his mother), and remembers a trip at the age of four when his mother threatened to leave him with the hotel manager; he runs to her crying, arms outstretched; she comforts him, swearing she was joking, while the manager snickers and calls him “mama's baby” Words: The mother: if he does not behave, she will leave and give him to the manager. The manager: “mama's baby” Atmosphere: Lingering pain in the arm while typing the report; a memory surfacing as if it were yesterday; the experimenter himself says he is skeptical: “All this may be cooked up” Stakes: The body as archive: a physical pain of today restores a scene decades old, never recalled since

During a muscle-tension experiment, the muscles at the corner of his mouth twist upward; for ten minutes he thinks it is a smile, then understands that it is the prelude to a fit of tears; he cries, for the first time since childhood; embarrassment interrupts the process; he connects the episode to his mother's death two years earlier, when he had wanted to cry and could not Atmosphere: Embarrassment at his own behavior; then, after the experiment, a feeling of well-being and extreme joy at having made this action available Stakes: The tears held back at his mother's funeral are released through a simple facial twitch two years later

The student, a notorious gobbler who reads at the table, observes that he bites partway and then tears off the rest; concentrating on the bite sends him off into reverie, and the mouthful is swallowed before he notices. He chews and chews: the back of his tongue hurts, he runs short of air, holds his breath, has to push the food to the sides, make empty swallowing movements, breathe deeply, then take up the leftovers again. After two mouthfuls the taste becomes hateful, he deliberately desensitizes himself, feels a strong urge to vomit, slips into reverie telling himself he must not spoil a whole meal, and stops, twice. Words: He tells himself not to spoil a whole meal by getting sick; there is a limit. He notes that this is obviously a resistance. Atmosphere: A mouth in disarray, a sore tongue, breath cut short, rising nausea, the stupor of reverie as an escape Stakes: The body defends itself against the experiment that would free it; resistance wins, lucidly acknowledged

She tries on a dress seen in Vogue or Harper's Bazaar; the mirror does not give back her long, supple, blond ideal; furious and disgusted with herself, she vows to diet; then, seized with self-pity, she sits down and eats candy or a piece of cake. Atmosphere: A cycle of self-hatred and sugary consolation Stakes: The introject of the ideal figure swallowed from magazines dominates her relation to food

The student, stretched out on floor and bench, looks for the introjects he carries: he thinks of tolerance, then out comes “How I hate her!”: fists clenched, biceps contracted, lips pressed together, teeth clenched, brows knitted, temples throbbing, ears pulled back, his whole body pressing against the floor and the bench; the tension and the burning in his stomach rise to the point of nausea; then comes the name “Aunt Agnes” and all the tensions vanish, leaving only a sour taste for a few minutes. Words: “How I hate her!” then “Aunt Agnes!”, words uttered with violent insistence Atmosphere: concentrated muscular violence, inner burning, then sudden release Stakes: the ejection of an introject embodied by a domineering, mannish aunt who had charge of him at age three

The eating experiments keep bringing the student's father to mind: a domineering man who wants to keep his children from growing up, for whom being a parent is his life's work more than his profession, and from which he never intends to retire. The student begins to vomit up the ideas forced into him, discovering how many views he took for his own were his father's; he feels immense relief in getting rid of them. Words: He says he analyzes his father's ideas in terms of present-day social and moral views and feels “a tremendous relief in sloughing off some of them” Stakes: the disassimilation of an introjected father

Looking for the introjects lodged in him like foreign bodies, the subject thinks back over the work on confluence (features, speech, bearing imitated from whom?) and comes to the problem of tolerance. Then out comes “How I hate her!”, the words “I” and “her” hammered out, fists clenched, biceps contracted, lips pressed together, teeth clenched, brows knitted, temples pounding, ears pulled back, his whole body crushed against the floor and the bench. At the same time, the tension in his stomach and a slight burning grow worse, to the point of nausea. Then come the words “Aunt Agnes!”, and all the tensions, burnings, pressures, and throbbings disappear; all that remains, for a few minutes, is a sour taste in his mouth. Words: “How I hate her!” then “Aunt Agnes!” Atmosphere: Mounting somatic violence, nausea, then instant release Stakes: A childhood hatred swallowed twenty years earlier, returned to the body and named: the past dislodged from a character trait

A constructed example: one is eating a steak; if one thinks it resembles last week's, this stirs up disgust; what matters is that it is steak in general and gives off its own new smell. Atmosphere: didactic, sensory Stakes: illustrating the difference between neurotic repetition and a healthy appetite turned toward novelty

A man is struck by a passing face; suddenly he feels an alien emotion, a strange attraction, a nameless grief, at once cut off by the present inhibition, which goes on. Atmosphere: brief, dizziness, a break Stakes: showing that an image that comes first, without any relaxing of the inhibition, remains empty and evanescent

The powerful patient, finishing an exercise, grows anxious at the moment of drawing something from it; asked about his self-reproaches, he admits that he wants to scold the therapist; he then accuses the therapist of exploiting the session, admits he wants to be admired by him, is disgusted with the boring experiments, and falls silent; in the silence he feels his jaw clenched and aching, remembers that his voice came out between his teeth, clenches them, then smiles on seeing his own dependence; working back along the chain, he thinks of other women, blames his upbringing, recognizes his mother's censorious face, concludes ironically that what people don't know can't hurt them, and decides to do the experiment again. Words: The therapist asks whom he would like to reproach instead of him; the patient asks whether he is really attractive to the therapist, and who is playing a game. Atmosphere: Mounting tension, the therapist's silence, a clenched jaw, anger, and a final smile. Stakes: Showing the step-by-step dissolution of layers of defense until contact is regained.

Chaet arrives from Boston, canvases under her arm on Albers's instructions; Albers examines the paintings and gives a remarkable critique; he asks insistently how Chaet would teach; after an hour and a half, he hires her on the spot Words: Albers: “bring the paintings”; then, about the critique, Chaet had never heard anyone talk that way; “no committees” Atmosphere: Direct, with no intermediary, dazzling for the young painter Stakes: Albers's absolute power and his way of exercising it
A work pairing a poem by Oppenheimer with an ink drawing by Rauschenberg, commemorating a dance by Katherine Litz performed in New York.

Rauschenberg takes out the still-wet canvas, lays it on the ground outside, and treats it as an adhesive surface or light-sensitive photographic paper: dust, earth, and gravel stick to it, black on black. Atmosphere: Tactile, nocturnal (Night Blooming), the gesture of a painter-photographer Stakes: The invention of the gesture that will lead from the Black Paintings to the combine paintings

A jealous student asks Tworkov why he spends so much time with Bob, who never comes to class. Words: Tworkov: it is when students stop coming to class that they interest him. Atmosphere: Benevolent irony Stakes: What the college makes of the students who do not attend

Litz leaps onto the stage, making the top of her tube dress float; she disappears and reappears six times behind the panel, galloping, pivoting, shuffling, crawling; a mermaid becomes a tree, then a stone sculpture, then an animal; bells ring out of sync, piano notes linger after she disappears. Atmosphere: mimic humor, precision, percussive variations Stakes: the reinvention of the body as a living glyph

Asawa explains Albers's Paper Fold; Renk does the exercises, learns the rules of folding, then persists for two days and two nights designing and folding an egg-carton shape. Words: Renk, remembering school: he had found neither children nor solutions; after Asawa: he had learned the basic rules of folding. Atmosphere: Joyful obsession, a night of work. Stakes: The passing on of Albers's teaching from one artist to another.
